title: Being “a man after God’s heart” never meant flawless behavior.
paragraphs: Being “a man after God’s heart” never meant flawless behavior.
It meant a heart that returns.
Look at King David—the man God Himself highlighted.

He defeated giants.
He wrote psalms that still shake hearts today.
But he also fell—hard.

Adultery.
Deception.
Murder.

Not rumors. Not exaggerations.
Documented sin.
So why would God still call him “a man after My own heart”? (Acts 13:22)
Here’s the tension…

It wasn’t because David never sinned.
It was because David never ran from God when he did.

When confronted, David didn’t justify.
He didn’t spin the narrative.
He didn’t blame the pressure.
He broke.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…” (Psalm 51:10)
That’s the difference.

Not perfection…
But repentance.

Not sinlessness…
But surrender.
Because the truth is—

Sin separates.
But repentance restores.
And this is where the Gospel gets real…
David’s story points forward to Jesus Christ—the only One who was perfect.

Where David failed, Jesus didn’t.
Where we fall, Jesus stands.
And then He does something scandalous—

He takes our sin, our failure, our hidden guilt…
And nails it to the cross.
So that through repentance and faith—
We don’t just get forgiven…
We get a new heart.
That’s what being after God’s heart really means.

Not someone who never falls—
But someone who always comes back.

Reflection:
When you fall, do you hide from God—or run toward Him?
This isn’t the end of your story.
